name: Progressive Disclosure
description: Presenting only the information or controls needed for the immediate task, deferring less-common options and complexity to secondary views revealed on request, on the working assumption that simplifying what's shown up front improves usability without removing capability.
design_relevance_note: The standard justification for hiding advanced settings behind an 'Advanced' toggle, collapsing detail behind 'Show more,' and staging onboarding/setup one decision at a time instead of a single dense form.
prevalence_note: One of the most frequently invoked interaction-design principles in practice -- routine justification for settings hierarchies, onboarding flows, and 'advanced options' patterns industry-wide.

findings.description: Across four studies extending their prior work, Springer & Whittaker found the benefit of transparency feedback in an intelligent system is context-dependent: transparency helps users build a working model of how the algorithm operates, but can simultaneously undermine perceived accuracy when it reveals algorithmic errors; users were more likely to consult and benefit from transparency information specifically when it helped them build that operational model, again motivating progressive-disclosure principles (initially simplified feedback that hides potential errors while users build working heuristics).
findings.source_title: Progressive Disclosure: When, Why, and How Do Users Want Algorithmic Transparency Information?
findings.source_venue: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems

findings.description: In two studies of a prototype intelligent 'emotional analytics' system, Springer & Whittaker found that users initially anticipated a more transparent version of the system would perform better, but retracted that favorable evaluation after actually using it; qualitative data indicated the added transparency was distracting and undermined the simple operating heuristics users tried to form, motivating a progressive-disclosure design principle of initially simplified feedback with complexity revealed only as needed.
findings.source_title: Progressive disclosure: empirically motivated approaches to designing effective transparency
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '19)

applications.title: The near-universal print dialog box: NN/g's canonical progressive-disclosure example
applications.description: Jakob Nielsen's Nielsen Norman Group article on progressive disclosure (published December 3, 2006) uses the operating-system print dialog box as its primary illustration: issuing a print command surfaces only a small set of immediately relevant choices (number of copies, which printer, whether to print the full document or a range), with rarely-needed settings (page scaling, reverse-order printing, etc.) deferred behind an 'advanced options' control rather than shown upfront. The article frames this as a near-universal convention across desktop operating systems and applications precisely because it resolves the tension between two conflicting user needs -- simplicity for the common case and full power for the rare case -- without sacrificing either.
applications.industry_context: Desktop operating-system UI conventions generally, not one specific product.
applications.ethical_note: A pure usability/information-architecture technique with no persuasive or manipulative dimension -- the intent is exclusively to reduce cognitive load for the common case while preserving full functionality for the rare one, not to steer a decision the user wouldn't otherwise make.
